I'm mostly experimenting with Pi's at the moment, but they aren't exactly economical.

I'm not sure about specific links, but here's an overall path I'd recommend:

  • Pick some simple projects that require simple tools: a breadboard, some electronics components, and an Arduino. Eventually you'll want a soldering station and a fan to suck up the fumes, also solder, solder wick, and solder paste/flux.

  • When you can breadboard a design pick an EDA package like Kicad. Do schematic capture

  • Once your circuit diagram is complete, learn Kicad's footprint and PCB tool, called PCBNew

  • Upload your design (gerber files) to a place like oshpark or another cheap PCB fab. They'll take about a week or two and send you three boards for cheap ($5-$15 total, including shipping)

  • Experiment with PDIP for through-hole and 1206 or 0805 for SMD. SMD is actually easier and faster to solder once you get used to it

  • If you want more formalized education, check out MIT Open Courseware's EE courses. And pick up an international version of The Art of Electronics in particular, from a place like abebooks.com, or pirate it from gen.lib.rus.ec if you're cheap.

  • I recommend learning 3D design to make your own enclosures, and either getting a 3D printer, finding a local one (search for "local 3d printers") or using a professional (and more expensive) service like shapeways.com. I like to use SolidWorks, and there are academic discounts, or you can pirate it--what harm is caused to use it solely for learning purposes?
